videos.title: A crate of apples is not a crate of fruit: one list with two labels lets a lemon in, so a list you can write to must match its type exactly
An apple dispenser only hands apples out, so with out a Dispenser<Apple> passes as a Dispenser<Fruit>
The compost bin takes any fruit, so a Bin<Fruit> stands in for a Bin<Apple>: in flips the arrow
Erasure tears the label off; inline with reified copies it onto a note at every call
Add a subtype: the pattern switch stops compiling, the instanceof chain stays silent
A decorator wraps the same interface: the call goes in layer by layer, and the order of the layers changes the fee
A circuit breaker's three states live in one AtomicReference, and compare-and-set picks the single probe
Kotlin's inline pastes the function body and its lambda into the caller: no Function0, no interface call, no unboxing
A delegated property is a hidden delegate field plus a getter and setter that call getValue and setValue
A tour of the event library: a sealed model behind one parsing edge, a typed bus, and an API for Kotlin and Java
A value class is its own type to the compiler and a plain long at run time, boxed whenever it is used as another type
A box whose label wore off: List<*> reads as Any?, takes nothing in, and is not the drawer MutableList<Any?>
A strategy is the one decision you plug in: sort keeps the loop, and the comparator decides which quote goes first
A box of Any lets the wrong thing in and fails at the counter; Box<T> puts a blank on the label that each caller fills, and the compiler checks every put
A lambda with receiver runs inside its builder; a bare call goes to the nearest receiver that has it, and @DslMarker stops it there
A group answers the same question as a single rule by asking its children, so one recursive function prices the whole fee plan
A request runs along a chain of checks until one answers, and the order of the list is behavior; then a payment's state decides which event is legal
The ledger tells a list of listeners, each in its own try; a command is an object on an undo stack, pushed only after it worked
A List runs each step over every payment; a Sequence pulls one payment through the whole chain and stops early, but sorted() still reads everything
Two questions pick a scope function: this or it, the object or the block's result, and why ?.let { } ?: run { } can run both blocks
Errors as values: fail fast stops at the first error, collecting runs every check, and runCatching swallows the cancel
A pure core decides from plain values, a thin shell does the I/O, and its inputs must not change underneath it
A pure function is like a recipe card: same ingredients, same result, kitchen left as it was; a hidden clock or global breaks it
A closure is a recipe card with a note pinned on, and a captured var is one shared box, so two threads lose updates on it
Pass in the work, not its answer: retry takes the call as a function, so one loop serves every flaky call
fold carries one reading past every cookie, like a jar on the kitchen scale; reduce has no start and throws on an empty day
For this job, take-only: Array<out Fruit> lets one function read a busy crate, while Java arrays only find out at run time
Visitor stores the type-by-job grid by column and reaches a cell in two hops; a sealed switch does it in one
A plain T can only do what Any? does; an upper bound such as T : Fruit is a fruit-only sign that shuts some callers out and lets the body weigh and compare
A sealed type puts its list of subtypes into the type, so javac checks every switch, and a new subtype breaks each one without a default
A base-class setter forgets the subclass; with B : Builder<B> each kind of form writes its own name in the blank, so grams returns a GiftBoxBuilder and the chain keeps ribbon
Checkout asks a factory for a gateway and never names the class; when an authorizer and a refunder must match, one call picks the whole card-network family
An adapter has your port's shape on one side and the SDK's on the other and translates calls, answers and errors; a facade is one front door that owns the order of the steps and the undo
A copy copies the arrow, not the object: two carts share one list until the list can't change and a change builds a new one; named and default arguments replace most builders
An object knows only its class: KClass and Class are one note on two kinds of paper, and only a KType, written by the compiler at a call site, keeps the whole label
Eight threads ask for the one price list and get eight; an enum, the holder idiom or double-checked locking makes the others wait, and the best singleton is passed in
Typed keys: the key carries its value's type, so a read needs no cast and same-named keys don't collide, and the key stays invariant because it writes too
A record is its components and javac writes the rest; the canonical constructor is the one door every instance passes, and immutability stops at the list a field points to
The compiler smart-casts only from what it can see and never opens a function you call; a contract writes the guarantee on the outside, and the compiler believes it without checking

A proxy must subclass your class, and Kotlin classes are final; a compiler plugin changes what kotlinc emits: all-open drops final, no-arg adds a hidden empty constructor, serialization writes a serializer class

One optional-field class allows 48 shapes and 3 make sense; three records under a sealed interface allow only those 3, one parse at the edge lets nothing else in, and the logic lives in functions over the data
One publish looks up the event's class, then each event supertype, nearest first, and a Handler declared in lets one general handler fit any subscription

Java sees only the class file: default arguments, a reified subscribe, object members and value classes each look odd or go missing there, and Class overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and a facade that still validates fix them
